newsitem.title: USA: Falling milk prices should bring smiles to consumers.
newsitem.headline: Falling milk prices should bring smiles to consumers.

text.p: Celebrities wear milk moustaches in the popular dairy ads, but consumers may soon be wearing smiles because milk prices are expected to fall in coming months.
Milk prices hit record highs late last year because of high feed costs. But, with feed prices easing, wholesale milk prices have fallen more than 25 percent from 1996 highs.
"There will be a substantial decline (in milk prices) over the next several months," said Ed Jesse, a University of Wisconsin dairy economist.

Average wholesale milk prices peaked at a record $16.30 per hundredweight, about $1.40 per gallon, in September but have since dropped to $11.34, or 97 cents per gallon, industry officials said. Milk processors use the average milk price to determine the price paid to milk producers.

Chris Nubern, an economist at the National Milk Producers Federation, said there is about a two-month delay before changes in the wholesale price are seen at supermarkets. As a result, the recent drop in wholesale prices should appear on supermaket shelves in February.
"The milk price outlook indicates prices will be lower than in 1996, but higher than 1995," said Jesse.
The Agriculture Department reported wholesale milk averaged $14.75 per hundredweight, $1.25 per gallon, in 1996 and $12.74 per hundredweight, or $1.08 per gallon, in 1995.
Milk prices could rebound later this year, however, if floods in California, the nation's leading milk producer, disrupt production and hay prices remain high in the Midwest, Jesse noted.
The Agriculture Department estimates annual milk production at 155.4 billion pounds from Oct. 1, 1996, to Sept. 30, 1997, up from 154.445 billion the previous year.
The National Milk Producers Federation in Arlington, Va., said milk production will exceed demand in 1997.

"We are going to produce a little more milk than we have a market for," said Ed Coughlin, director of regulatory affairs at the federation. The group represents dairy farmers who produce about 60 percent of the nation's milk.
The fall in milk prices has angered some dairy farmers, who have conducted brief protests. But dairy industry officials said the protests are not gaining widespread support.
